metadata.goal: Identify overall situation across all usages for morning and evening rush hours and find some anomalies during this period.
metadata.category: Rush-hour usage, speed, route directness, destination land-use, and spatial anomalies
metadata.header: MTL Trajet: 08 Rush-hour Usage Destination Anomalies
metadata.dataset_description: MTL urban trajectories with usage, rush-hour timing, route directness, speed, destination land-use, endpoints, and timestamped point records.
metadata.metric_note: `route_directness_ratio` is route length divided by straight-line distance; values closer to 1 indicate more direct trajectories.
metadata.map_context_note: The destination-land-use visualization uses a static OpenStreetMap background only as geographic context; the plotted destination coordinates are from the supplied case tables.
metadata.land_use_reference: Archived PUM2050 Affectatio polygons (2025). Labels describe reference-map zoning at fixed endpoints, not surveyed activities at the time of travel.
metadata.motion_consistency_note: Point speed is the incoming segment GPS great-circle distance divided by elapsed time; the first point repeats the first outgoing segment speed. Earth radius: 6371.0088 km. Trip distance is the sum of these segment distances. avg_speed_kmh and mean_speed_kmh are total distance / elapsed time; avg_point_speed_kmh and point_speed_mean_kmh are unweighted means of the delivered point speeds. speed_cv is the population coefficient of variation of incoming segment speeds, excluding the duplicated first endpoint. trajectory_progress is point_index / (point_count - 1), not elapsed-time fraction. Timestamps and speed fields were reconstructed for internal consistency on 2026-10-09; GPS positions and insight wording were preserved. These are curated example records, not newly recovered observations.

Speed distributions are generally similar across usage groups, whereas route-directness distributions vary across them.

summary: Work and education account for the largest shares of rush-hour trips. Speed distributions are generally similar across usage groups, whereas route-directness distributions vary across them. Most trajectories end in Mixte destinations in the city-center area. A small number of health-related trajectories are unusually direct and travel from the city center to outside the city.
evidence_policy: Claims describe patterns in this dataset and do not establish causal relationships.
